newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croatia's Tudjman visits rebel Serb enclave.
newsitem.headline: Croatia's Tudjman visits rebel Serb enclave.

text.p: Croatian President Franjo Tudjman on Tuesday visited the country's Eastern Slavonia region for the first time since it was seized by rebel Serbs in 1991 during Croatia's war of independence from Yugoslavia.

The Croatian news agency HINA said Tudjman's unannounced visit included the town of Vukovar, which was destroyed by the Yugoslav Army in a three-month siege before U.N. peacekeepers separated the two sides.

Douglas Koffman, spokesman for the U.N.'s Transitional Administration for Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES), said Tudjman made "a quick tour of Vukovar", accompanied by UNTAES head, U.S. General Jacques Klein.
After its fall, Vukovar became an emotive symbol of Croatia's determination to recover all territory lost to the Serbs.
Zagreb recaptured other Serb enclaves in military action last year, but agreed to hang fire on Eastern Slavonia and try a peaceful approach.
Tudjman visited a mass grave at Ovcara near Vukovar, from which U.N. forensic experts recovered some 200 bodies, believed to be Croatian civilians executed by conquering Serb troops in November 1991.
He also toured three villages in the south, where Croatian refugees expelled five years ago, were to return before Christmas, in another boost to the peaceful reintegration of the enclave.
Tudjman and Klein discussed problems related to Zagreb's taking over the fertile, oil-rich area, due to take place next year, Koffman said.
HINA said Tudjman also met local Serb leaders, who have visited Zagreb to pledge their support to the reintegration.
The reintegration, which only began this year, has been frought with lingering antagonism and suspicion among the Serbs, who fear persecution under Croatian rule.
Analysts said Tudjman's visit appeared to be motivated by a desire to score important points ahead of presidential and local elections due next year.
The 74-year-old president returned home from Washington last week, where he underwent medical treatment for what U.S. sources said was stomach cancer.
His ruling HDZ party is facing a huge decline in popularity and the government has been the target of mass protests by pensioners, public sector and railway workers demanding more money.
